directives.description: To make the assembled machine code run on a C64 or in an emulator, it's useful to include a little basic program that starts your code (for example: 10 sys 4096). The BasicUpstart macro is standard macro that helps you to create programs like that.
examples:
*= $0801 'Basic Upstart'
BasicUpstart(start) // 10 sys$0810
*= $0810 'Program'
start: inc $d020
inc $d021
jmp start

BasicUpstart2(start) // 10 sys$0810
start: inc $d020
inc $d021
jmp start

directives.description: Defines a constant. A constant can't be assigned a new value. Note that not all values are immutable. If you define a constant that points to a list, the content of the list can still change. If you want to make a mutable value immutable, you can use its lock() function, which will lock it's content
examples: .const x=25 //Defines a constant x with a value of 25

directives.description: Defines a variable. With variables you can store data for later use. Before you can use a variable you have to declare it. You do this with the .var directive
examples: .var c=1                 // Declares the variable c to be 1
.var name = "MYSTRING" // Variables can assume any value, for example string

directives.description: The .eval directive is used to make Kick Assembler evaluate expressions. In fact, the .var directive above is just a convenient shorthand of ".eval var x =25", where var is a subexpression that declares a variable.
examples: .eval x=x+10 // Adds 10 to whatever is in variable x

directives.description: With the .enum statement you can define enumerations, which are series of constants.
examples: .enum {up,down,left,right, none=$ff} // You can mix implicit and explicit

directives.description: Label declarations in Kick Assembler end with ":" and have no postfix when referred to. You can put labels in front of mnemonic arguments. This can be useful when creating self modifying code. Kick Assembler also supports multi labels, which are labels that can be declared more than once. These are useful to prevent name conflicts between labels. A multi label starts with a **!** and when your reference it you have to end with a **+** to refer to the next multi label or **-** to refer to the previous multi label.
The .byte, .word, .dword and .text directives are used to generate byte, word (one word= two bytes), dword (double word = 4 bytes) and text data as in standard 65xx assemblers.

With the .fill directive you can fill a section of the memory with bytes. It works like a loop and automatically sets the variable i to the iteration number.

With the .import directive you can import **data** from external files into your code. You can import binary, C64, and text files. To import Kick Assembler source files see the #import preprocessor directive. The binary, c64 and text import takes an offset and a length as optional parameters.
examples: .import binary "Music.bin" // import the bytes from the file 'music.bin'
.import c64 "charset.c64" // (Same as binary but skips the first two address bytes)
.import binary "Music.bin", 100 // import the bytes from the file 'music.bin', but skip the first 100 bytes
.import c64 "charset.c64", $400, $200 // Imports $200 bytes starting from position $402

directives.description: With the .print directive you can output text to the user while assembling.
You can define your own functions which you can use like any of the build in library functions.
Pseudo commands are a special kind of macros that take command arguments, like #20, table,y or ($30),y as arguments just like mnemonics do. With these you can make your own extended commands.

You can define you own functions which you can use like any of the build in library functions. Functions consist of non-byte generating directives like .eval, .for, .var, and .if. When the assembler evaluates the .return directive it returns the value given by the proceeding expression. If no expression is given, or if no .return directive is reached, a null value is returned. You can have several functions of the same name, as long as they have a different number of arguments.
examples: // Returns a string telling if a number is odd or even

directives.description: Used inside functions to return a value. When the assembler evaluates the .return directive it returns the value given by the proceeding expression. If no expression is given, or if no .return directive is reached, a null value is returned.
examples: // Returns a string telling if a number is odd or even

directives.description: Namespaces are containers of functions, macros and pseudocommands. There can only be one of each of these entities in namespace. Every namespace also have an its own associated scope so each time you define a namespace a scopes is automatically defined. A simple way to declare a namespace is shown in the following example. The namespace directives is covered in more detail later (and often the .filenamespace directive is more handy)

Macros are collections of assembler directives. When called, they generate code as if the directives where placed at the macro call. A macro can have any number of arguments. Macro calls are encapsulated in a scope, hence any variable defined inside a macro can't be seen from directly the outside. This means that a series of macro calls to the same macro doesn't interfere
examples: SetColor(2)   // The colon in front of macro calls is optional from version 4.0

directives.description: With the .align directive, you can align the program counter to a given interval. This is useful for optimizing your code as crossing a memory page boundary yields a penalty of one cycle for memory referring commands. To avoid this, use the .align command to align your tables
examples: .align $100   //Alignment to the nearest page boundary saves a cycle

directives.description: Assert directives are useful for testing. They were made to make it easy to test the assembler itself, but you can use them for testing your own pseudo-commands, macros, functions. When assertions are used, the assembler will automatically count the number of assertions and the number of failed assertions and display these when the assembling has finished. With the assert directive you can test the value of expressions. .assert takes three arguments: a description, an expression, and an expected result.

Asserts that a given expression or codeblock generates an error. Like the assert directive the asserterror directive also has a form that can assert code. o make sure that an expression gives an error when the user gives the wrong parameters to a function, use the .asserterror directive.

The .break directive puts a breakpoint on the current memory position. You can add an argument to a breakpoint. The syntax of this argument is dependant on the consumer. For example .break 'if y<5' is written for VICE's conditional expressions. VICE will then break if the y register is below 5
examples: .break         // This will put a breakpoint on 'inc $d020

directives.description: Kick Assembler supports different sets of opcodes. The default set includes the standard 6502 mnemonics plus the illegal opcodes. To switch between instruction sets of different cpu's use the .cpu directive.
examples: .cpu _6502             // The standard 6502 instruction + the illegal opcodes. This is the default setting for KickAssembler.
.cpu dtv               // The standard 6502 instruction set + the DTV commands

directives.description: If-directives work like in standard programming languages. With an .if directive you have the proceeding directive executed only if a given boolean expression is evaluated to true. You can group several statements together in a block with {…} and have them executed together. By adding an else statement you can have an expression executed if the boolean expression is false.
examples: // Add the x'th entry of a table if x is positive or
// subtract it if x is negative
// Init an offset table or display a warning if the table length is exceeded

directives.description: The else keyword is used with .if directives to specify code that should be executed when the if condition is false. It must follow an .if block.
For-loops in Kick Assembler work similar to for-loops in C/Java. The .for directive allows you to repeat a block of code with a loop variable that changes on each iteration.
The .while directive executes as long as a given expressions is true. That is, it works like a .for-loop but without the init and iteration parameters.
An alias for '.byte'. Outputs bytes.
An alias for '.word'. Outputs words (two byte values).
An alias for '.dword'. Outputs doublewords (4 byte values).
An alias for '.text'. Dumps text bytes to memory.

Executes a block of directives in 'functionmode' (faster) to define values. In functionmode, only non-byte-generating directives are allowed. This is useful for defining many constants or variables efficiently.
Creates a d64 image file. You can specify disk parameters such as name and id, and include files in the disk image.
Sets the character encoding used by the .text directive. Kick Assembler supports several encodings including petscii_mixed, petscii_upper, screencode_mixed, and screencode_upper.
Creates a user raised error. Use this directive to stop the assembler with an error message when an invalid condition is detected.
Creates a user raised error if the given condition is evaluated to true. This is a shorthand for .if(condition) .error "message".
Creates a prg or bin file from the given segments. This directive is used when working with segments to control which segments are written to which output files.
Modifies the output of the current source file with the given modifier. This can be used to apply transformations like encryption or compression to the entire file output.
Creates a namespace for all the following directives in the current source file. This is often more convenient than the .namespace directive when you want an entire file to be in a namespace.
examples: // All labels, macros, functions in this file are now in 'mylib'

directives.description: Fills a number of words with the value of a given expression. Works like .fill but generates 16-bit word values instead of bytes.
Makes the assembler skip the current file if it has already been imported. Place this at the top of library files to prevent duplicate inclusion. (Deprecated, use #importonce instead)
examples: // Rest of the library file follows

directives.description: Fills two tables with the hi and lo byte of the given expression. This is very useful for creating address lookup tables commonly needed in C64 programming.
examples: // Creates a lo-byte table followed by a hi-byte table

directives.description: Defines a new memoryblock at the current memory position. Memory blocks are used to organize output data.
Modifies the output of a codeblock using the given modifier. Unlike .filemodify which affects the whole file, .modify only affects the enclosed code block.
Sets the program counter to a given value. This is an alternative syntax for '*=' (set memory position).
Tells the assembler to look for a plugin at the given Java package path. Plugins can extend Kick Assembler with custom functionality written in Java.
Sets the program counter to something else than the actual memory position. This is useful when code will be relocated at runtime to a different address than where it is initially loaded.
examples: // Code assembled at current position but addresses calculated for $2000

directives.description: Switches to another segment. Segments allow you to organize your code and data into logical blocks that can be placed at different memory locations.
examples: .segment Code []  // Switch back to Code segment

directives.description: Defines a segment. You must define a segment before you can switch to it. Segment definitions specify properties like start address, maximum size, and whether it should be written to the output.
Outputs the bytes of an intermediate segment to the current memoryblock. This is used to embed one segment's output within another segment.
Creates a user defined structure. Structures group related data fields together and can be used to create organized data layouts.
Marks unresolved labels as being in the zeropage. This allows the assembler to use the more efficient zeropage addressing mode for labels whose address is not yet known at the time of use.

preprocessorStatements.description: Use the preprocessor to import other **source** files. To import **data** files see the .import directive.
Use the preprocessor to import other **source** files. To import **data** files see the .import directive.
examples: #importif STAND_ALONE "UpstartCode.asm" // Only import "UpstartCode.asm" if STAND_ALONE is defined

preprocessorStatements.description: The preprocessor uses symbols do determine if it should discard or include portions of the source file. There are two methods to define a symbol. The first is from the command line. The other way is using the #define directive.
If you want to remove the definition of a symbol previously defined with #define, use the #undef directive.
Ensures that the current file will only be imported once. Place this at the top of library files to prevent duplicate imports when the file is referenced from multiple sources.
examples: #importonce  // Place at top of library file

preprocessorStatements.description: Conditional compilation. Excludes the following source code if the given expression evaluates to false. The expression can test preprocessor symbols defined with #define or from the command line.
Combines #else and #if for chained conditional compilation. Tests a new condition if the previous #if or #elif was false.
Introduces an alternative block within a conditional compilation structure. The code after #else is compiled only when the preceding #if or #elif condition was false.
Closes an active #if, #elif, or #else conditional compilation block.
